chunks: Muhammad ibn Abdullah narrated to me from his father, from Abu Abdillah al-Barqi, from some of our companions, who said:

A woman gave me some yarn and asked me to give it to the keepers of the Ka'bah to use it to make the cover of the Ka'bah. I said: I disliked giving it to the keepers while I knew them. When we arrived in Medina, I entered upon Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) and said to him: May I be sacrificed for you, a woman gave me some yarn and asked me to give it in Mecca to be used to make the cover of the Ka'bah, so I disliked giving it to the keepers. He said: Buy honey and saffron with it, and take from the clay of the grave of Husayn (peace be upon him) and knead it with rainwater, and put some of the honey and saffron in it, and distribute it among the Shia so that they may cure their ill ones with it.

key_terms.حَجَبَةِ مَكَّةَ: keepers or custodians of the Ka'bah
key_terms.طِينِ قَبْرِ الْحُسَيْنِ: clay of the grave of Husayn

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on using the clay of Imam Husayn's grave for healing according to this hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Kamil al-Ziyarat* highlights the practical authority of the Imams in managing charitable endowments (sadaqat), illustrating how Imam al-Baqir (a.s.) redirected material wealth from the Ka'bah's cover to a more immediate spiritual and physical benefit for the Shia community. The preparation of a medicinal paste using the grave's clay, honey, and saffron underscores the Shia belief in the barakah (blessing) inherent in the Ahl al-Bayt's physical remains, serving as both a cure for illness and a means of strengthening communal bonds.
